title: Spanish
description: A practical first course in Spanish for absolute beginners who want to actually speak and understand the language. You will master pronunciation, the core grammar patterns that carry most everyday speech, and the vocabulary for real situations like meeting people, describing your family, ordering food, shopping, and talking about the past.
outcomes: You can pronounce Spanish vowels, consonants, and stress patterns accurately, including rr, ñ, j, and accent marks.
You can greet people, introduce yourself, and choose correctly between ser and estar for identity, description, location, and condition.
You can build correct noun phrases with proper gender, number, articles, and agreeing adjectives.
You can conjugate regular -ar, -er, and -ir verbs in the present tense and form questions and negative sentences.
You can handle real situations — ordering food, shopping, asking directions — using numbers, time expressions, and everyday vocabulary.
You can describe a completed past event using the preterite, including common irregular verbs like ir, ser, hacer, and tener.

units.title: Sounds and First Words
units.summary: Spanish spelling is far more consistent than English's, so pronunciation work up front pays off immediately. This unit covers the sound system and the phrases you need for a first conversation.

lessons.title: The Spanish Alphabet and Pronunciation
lessons.intro: Spanish is written almost exactly the way it sounds, so once you learn its few rules, you can read any new word aloud correctly on the first try — a rare gift among languages.

sections.heading: Five Pure Vowels
body: Spanish has exactly five vowel sounds, and each one is always pronounced the same way, unlike English vowels, which shift constantly depending on the word. *a* sounds like the 'a' in 'father,' *e* like the 'e' in 'bet,' *i* like the 'ee' in 'see,' *o* like the 'o' in 'boat' with no glide, and *u* like the 'oo' in 'boot.'

Because vowels never change sound, *casa* (house) is always 'KAH-sah,' never 'KAY-suh.' This consistency means spelling tells you exactly how to pronounce a word, and hearing a word tells you exactly how to spell it — a real advantage over English.

sections.heading: Tricky Consonants: rr, ñ, j, ll
body: The letter *ñ* adds an 'ny' sound, as in *año* (year), pronounced 'AH-nyoh' — confusing it with *ano* changes the meaning entirely. A single *r* between vowels is a quick tongue tap, like the American 'tt' in 'butter,' while *rr*, and *r* at the start of a word, is a rolled, trilled r, as in *perro* (dog).

*J* is pronounced like a harsh English 'h,' so *jugo* (juice) sounds like 'HOO-goh.' *G* makes that same harsh sound before *e* or *i* (*gente* = 'HEN-teh') but a hard 'g' before *a*, *o*, or *u* (*gato* = 'GAH-toh'). In most of Latin America, *ll* and *y* both sound like the English 'y,' so *llamo* sounds like 'YAH-moh.'

sections.heading: Stress and the Accent Mark
body: Spanish stress follows two default rules: words ending in a vowel, *n*, or *s* stress the second-to-last syllable (ha-BLAN), while words ending in any other consonant stress the last syllable (ha-BLAR). Whenever a word breaks these rules, a written accent mark shows exactly where the stress falls.

That's why *hablo* (I speak) and *habló* (he/she spoke) look almost identical but sound different and mean different things — the accent on the o shifts the stress and the tense. Spotting accent marks is not decoration; it changes meaning.

example.problem: Where does the stress fall in *joven* (young) and *jamón* (ham), and why?
steps: *joven* ends in -n, so by the default rule stress falls on the second-to-last syllable: JO-ven.
*jamón* also ends in -n, but it carries a written accent on the ó, which overrides the default rule.
The accent moves the stress to the last syllable: ja-MÓN.
example.answer: JO-ven (default rule applies, no accent needed) and ja-MÓN (the accent overrides the default and forces stress onto the final syllable).

keyTerms.def: The syllable in a word pronounced with more emphasis; in Spanish, predictable from the last letter unless marked with an accent.
The wavy mark over ñ that changes it into a distinct 'ny' sound, different from plain n.
The rolled r sound written as rr, or as a single r at the start of a word.
A mark (´) placed over a vowel to override the default stress rule and show exactly where a word is stressed.

practice.q: How is the double r in *perro* pronounced?
practice.explain: rr (and initial r) is always a trilled/rolled sound in Spanish, distinct from the quick tapped r found between vowels.

practice.q: Which is the correctly spelled word for 'year'?
practice.explain: The tilde over ñ is required; año (year) uses ñ, while ano without the tilde is a different, unrelated word.

practice.q: Why does *hablo* mean 'I speak' but *habló* mean 'he/she spoke'?
choices: The written accent shifts the stress and changes the tense
They are actually the same word
practice.explain: The written accent overrides the default stress rule, moving stress to the final syllable and signaling a different verb form (the preterite).

lessons.title: Meeting People: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.intro: The first thirty seconds of any conversation in Spanish run on a small, predictable set of phrases — learn them well and you'll never freeze at 'hello.'

sections.heading: Hello, Goodbye, and Time of Day
body: Spanish greetings shift with the time of day: *buenos días* (good morning) is used until roughly midday, *buenas tardes* (good afternoon) covers afternoon into early evening, and *buenas noches* covers both 'good evening' and 'good night.' *Hola* (hi) works at any time, in almost any situation, formal or casual.

To say goodbye, *adiós* is the general word, while *hasta luego* (see you later) and *hasta mañana* (see you tomorrow) are common and slightly warmer. *Chao*, borrowed from Italian, is a casual goodbye heard throughout Latin America.

sections.heading: Introducing Yourself
body: To give your name, say *me llamo* + name (literally 'I call myself'), as in *Me llamo Ana*. To ask someone's name informally, ask *¿Cómo te llamas?*; to ask politely, or of a stranger, use *¿Cómo se llama usted?* On first meeting someone, *mucho gusto* ('a pleasure' / 'nice to meet you') is the standard reply.

You can also say *Soy* + name (*Soy Ana*, 'I am Ana'), using the verb *ser*, covered in the next lesson. Both *me llamo* and *soy* are completely natural, and native speakers use both interchangeably for introducing themselves.

sections.heading: Formal Tú vs Usted
body: Spanish has two words for singular 'you': *tú* (informal, used with friends, family, children, and peers) and *usted* (formal, used with strangers, elders, and in professional settings). The verb form changes depending on which one you use — this is the single most common way English speakers accidentally sound rude or overly stiff.

As a rule of thumb, use *usted* with anyone clearly older than you, in a business or service context, or the first time you meet someone formally; switch to *tú* once the other person invites it or the relationship turns casual. When in doubt, *usted* is always the safe choice.

example.problem: You are meeting your new boss for the first time at a job interview. Which form of 'you' should you use, and how would you ask their name?
steps: Recognize the context: a formal, professional first meeting with someone in authority.
A formal context calls for *usted*, not *tú*.
Ask: ¿Cómo se llama usted?
example.answer: Use usted — ¿Cómo se llama usted? — because the situation is formal and you don't yet know the person.

keyTerms.def: Good morning; used from waking until roughly midday.
'Nice to meet you,' said upon a first introduction.
The informal singular 'you,' used with friends, family, and peers.
The formal singular 'you,' used with strangers, elders, and in professional settings.

practice.q: Which greeting is appropriate at 8 PM?
practice.explain: Buenas noches covers both evening and night hours, unlike buenos días (morning) or buenas tardes (afternoon).

practice.q: Which is the informal way to ask someone's name?
practice.explain: Te llamas uses the informal tú form; se llama usted is the formal version for strangers or formal settings.

practice.q: You are checking in with a hotel receptionist you've never met. Which form of 'you' fits?
practice.explain: A first meeting with a stranger in a professional context calls for the formal usted, not the informal tú.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar: Two Verbs for 'To Be'
lessons.intro: English squeezes every meaning of 'to be' into one verb, but Spanish splits the job between ser and estar — mixing them up is the most common grammar mistake learners make, and getting it right instantly makes you sound fluent.

sections.heading: Ser: Identity and Characteristics
body: *Ser* (soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son) covers things that define what someone or something fundamentally is: identity, profession, nationality, physical traits, personality, origin, and clock time. *Soy profesora* (I am a teacher), *Es alto* (He is tall), and *Son las tres* (It is three o'clock) all describe facts that aren't expected to change moment to moment.

A handy memory device is DOCTOR: Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin, Relationship — all core ser categories. *Es de México* (She's from Mexico) uses ser for origin; *Es mi hermano* (He's my brother) uses it for relationship.

sections.heading: Estar: Location and Condition
body: *Estar* (estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están) covers location and temporary states: where something is, and how someone feels or is currently doing. *Estoy cansado* (I am tired) and *El libro está en la mesa* (The book is on the table) both describe a temporary or physical-position fact, not a defining trait.
Estar also forms the present progressive ('-ing' actions): *estoy comiendo* (I am eating). A useful shorthand is PLACE: Position, Location, Action, Condition, Emotion — all typical estar territory.

sections.heading: The Same Adjective, Two Meanings
body: Some adjectives change meaning depending on which verb pairs with them. *Es aburrido* (with ser) means 'he/she is boring' (a personality trait), while *Está aburrido* (with estar) means 'he/she is bored' (a temporary feeling) — the same adjective, opposite implication, depending on the verb.

Similarly, *Es rico* (with ser) means 'he is rich,' while *Está rico* (with estar, about food) means 'it's delicious.' Because the choice of verb genuinely changes the meaning of the sentence, ser/estar is not a minor detail to skip.

example.problem: Complete correctly: 'Mi abuela ___ inteligente' (a permanent trait) and 'Mi abuela ___ enferma hoy' (a temporary condition).
steps: 'Intelligent' describes a lasting personality trait, so use ser.
'Sick today' describes a temporary, changeable condition, so use estar.
Conjugate each for 'mi abuela' (she): es and está.
example.answer: Mi abuela es inteligente. Mi abuela está enferma hoy.

keyTerms.def: The 'to be' verb for identity, origin, characteristics, profession, relationships, and time — lasting or defining facts.
The 'to be' verb for location and temporary states, feelings, conditions, and ongoing actions.
A memory aid for ser: Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin, Relationship.
A memory aid for estar: Position, Location, Action, Condition, Emotion.

practice.q: Which verb fits: 'Yo ___ de Puerto Rico' (I am from Puerto Rico)?
practice.explain: Origin is a ser category (the O in DOCTOR); the correct yo-form of ser is soy.

practice.q: Which sentence means 'he is bored' rather than 'he is boring'?
practice.explain: Estar + aburrido describes a temporary feeling (bored); ser + aburrido describes a lasting trait (boring).

practice.q: Why is 'El café está caliente' (the coffee is hot) correct with estar rather than ser?
choices: Temperature is a temporary, changeable condition
Coffee is always defined by being hot
Ser is only used for people
practice.explain: A condition that can change moment to moment, like temperature, takes estar, not ser.

units.title: Nouns, Gender, and Articles
units.summary: Every Spanish noun carries a gender, and articles and adjectives must agree with it. This unit builds the noun-phrase skills used in every sentence from here on.

lessons.title: Gender and Number of Nouns
lessons.intro: Every single noun in Spanish is either masculine or feminine, even a table or a pencil, and getting the gender right changes almost every other word in the sentence.

sections.heading: Recognizing Gender by Ending
body: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (*el libro*, book) and most ending in -a are feminine (*la mesa*, table), covering a large share of everyday vocabulary. But there are well-known exceptions: *el día* (day) is masculine despite ending in -a, and *la mano* (hand) is feminine despite ending in -o, so the ending is a strong hint, not an absolute rule.

Nouns ending in -ción, -sión, -dad, and -tud are reliably feminine: *la nación* (nation), *la ciudad* (city), *la actitud* (attitude). When a noun's ending doesn't clearly signal gender, such as endings in -e or a consonant, it simply has to be memorized along with the noun itself.

sections.heading: Making Nouns Plural
body: To pluralize a noun ending in a vowel, add -s: *libro → libros*, *mesa → mesas*. To pluralize a noun ending in a consonant, add -es: *papel* (paper) → *papeles*, *ciudad → ciudades*.
A noun ending in -z changes the z to c before adding -es: *lápiz* (pencil) → *lápices*. This spelling change keeps the pronunciation smooth and applies consistently across every -z noun.

example.problem: Make 'la ciudad' (the city) and 'el lápiz' (the pencil) plural.
steps: Ciudad ends in a consonant, so add -es: ciudades.
Lápiz ends in -z, so change z→c and add -es: lápices.

keyTerms.def: A noun that takes el/un and typically, not always, ends in -o.
A noun that takes la/una and typically, not always, ends in -a, -ción, -dad, or -tud.
A noun whose gender doesn't match its typical ending, like el día or la mano, and must be memorized individually.
Adding -s after a vowel or -es after a consonant to make a noun plural; -z changes to -c before -es.

practice.q: Which of these is a well-known exception to the -o/-a gender rule?
practice.explain: El día (day) ends in -a but is masculine, one of the best-known gender exceptions in Spanish.

practice.q: What is the correct plural of 'el lápiz'?
practice.explain: Nouns ending in -z change to -c before adding -es: lápiz → lápices.

practice.q: Which ending reliably signals a feminine noun?
practice.explain: -dad (like -ción, -sión, and -tud) is a reliable feminine ending, as in la ciudad and la libertad.

lessons.title: Articles and Adjective Agreement
lessons.intro: Once you know a noun's gender and number, other words in the sentence have to match it — starting with the article and any adjective describing it.

sections.heading: Definite and Indefinite Articles
body: Definite articles ('the') are *el* (masc. sing.), *la* (fem. sing.), *los* (masc. pl.), *las* (fem. pl.). Indefinite articles ('a/an,' 'some') are *un* (masc. sing.), *una* (fem. sing.), *unos* (masc. pl.), *unas* (fem. pl.). *El libro* (the book), *unos libros* (some books), *la mesa* (the table), *unas mesas* (some tables).

One quirk: feminine singular nouns that start with a stressed a- or ha- sound use *el* instead of *la*, purely for pronunciation. *El agua* (the water) is still feminine, as shown by *el agua fría* (cold water) using the feminine adjective; it just borrows the masculine article to avoid two a-sounds colliding.

sections.heading: Adjectives Must Agree Too
body: Adjectives change their ending to match the gender and number of the noun they describe: *rojo* (red, masc. sing.) → *roja* (fem. sing.) → *rojos* (masc. pl.) → *rojas* (fem. pl.). Most descriptive adjectives are placed after the noun: *la casa roja* (the red house), not before it as in English.

Adjectives ending in -e or most consonants don't change for gender, only for number: *un carro grande* (a big car), *una casa grande* (a big house); grande stays the same for both, but adds -s for plural: *casas grandes*.

example.problem: Translate 'the red houses' and 'a big table,' matching all agreement correctly.
steps: Houses (casas) is feminine plural, so use las and make roja plural and feminine: rojas.
Table (mesa) is feminine singular, so use una; grande doesn't change for gender: grande.
example.answer: las casas rojas; una mesa grande.

keyTerms.def: 'The' in Spanish: el, la, los, las, matching the noun's gender and number.
'A/an' or 'some' in Spanish: un, una, unos, unas.
The requirement that an adjective's ending match the gender and number of the noun it describes.
Most Spanish descriptive adjectives follow the noun, unlike in English: casa roja, not roja casa.

practice.q: What is the correct plural of 'una mesa grande' (a big table)?
practice.explain: Both the article and the adjective must become plural and stay feminine: unas mesas grandes.

practice.q: Why does 'el agua' use el even though agua is feminine?
choices: To avoid two stressed a-sounds colliding at the start of the word
Because water is always masculine in Spanish
It is simply an error in the language
practice.explain: El replaces la only for pronunciation before a stressed a-/ha- sound; agua remains grammatically feminine, as shown by el agua fría.

practice.q: Where does a typical descriptive adjective go in a Spanish sentence?
choices: Only at the start of the sentence
practice.explain: Unlike English, most Spanish descriptive adjectives follow the noun they modify: la casa roja.

lessons.title: Subject Pronouns and Tener
lessons.intro: Tener (to have) is one of the most-used verbs in Spanish — it covers possession, age, and obligation, all with one irregular but very learnable pattern.

sections.heading: Subject Pronouns
body: Spanish subject pronouns are: *yo* (I), *tú* (you, informal), *él/ella/usted* (he/she/you formal), *nosotros/nosotras* (we), *vosotros/vosotras* (you all, Spain only), *ellos/ellas/ustedes* (they/you all). Because the verb ending already shows who's acting, Spanish speakers usually drop the pronoun entirely — you say *hablo*, not *yo hablo*, unless you want emphasis or contrast.

*Vosotros* is used only in Spain for informal 'you all'; almost everywhere in Latin America, *ustedes* covers both formal and informal plural 'you.' A beginner traveling in Latin America can safely skip vosotros and simply use ustedes.

sections.heading: Tener: To Have
body: Tener is irregular: *tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen*. Notice the e→ie change in every form except yo and nosotros/vosotros — this stem-change pattern reappears in many other common verbs, so learning it here pays off repeatedly.

Tener does double duty beyond possession. Spanish uses tener for age: *tengo veinte años* (I am twenty, literally 'I have twenty years'), not a form of 'to be.' *Tener que* + infinitive means 'to have to': *tengo que estudiar* (I have to study).

example.problem: Say in Spanish: 'She is 15 years old and has to work.'
steps: Age uses tener: tiene quince años (she has fifteen years).
'Has to' uses tener que + infinitive: tiene que trabajar.
example.answer: Tiene quince años y tiene que trabajar.

keyTerms.def: A pronoun like yo, tú, or ella that identifies who performs the verb's action; often omitted in Spanish since the verb ending already shows this.
'To have'; also used idiomatically for age (tener ... años) and obligation (tener que + infinitive).
A verb whose vowel changes in most forms, like tener's e→ie, but stays regular in nosotros/vosotros.
The informal 'you all' pronoun used in Spain; replaced by ustedes in Latin America.

practice.q: How do you say 'I am 20 years old' in Spanish?
practice.explain: Spanish expresses age with tener (to have), not ser or estar: tengo veinte años, literally 'I have twenty years.'

practice.q: What does 'tengo que estudiar' mean?
practice.explain: Tener que + infinitive expresses obligation: tengo que estudiar means 'I have to study.'

practice.q: Which pronoun is typically replaced by ustedes in Latin America?
practice.explain: Vosotros (informal you-all) is used only in Spain; Latin America uses ustedes for both formal and informal plural you.

units.title: Numbers, Time, and Family
units.summary: This unit adds the vocabulary that lets you handle dates, schedules, and describing the people closest to you.

lessons.title: Numbers 0-100
lessons.intro: Numbers show up everywhere — prices, ages, phone numbers, addresses — so fluency here pays off immediately in daily life.

sections.heading: Zero to Thirty
body: The numbers 0-15 are each their own word: *cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince*. From 16 to 29, the numbers fuse 'ten-and' into one word: *dieciséis* (16, diez y seis), *diecisiete* (17), *veintiuno* (21, veinte y uno), *veintidós* (22), and so on, with veinte (20) as the base.

Notice the accent marks that appear in this range purely to preserve stress: *dieciséis* and *veintidós* both carry accents so the stress lands correctly on the fused word. Getting to *treinta* (30) completes the first big milestone.

sections.heading: Thirty to a Hundred
body: From 31 onward, numbers stop fusing and instead use *y* (and) as a separate word: *treinta y uno* (31), *treinta y dos* (32). The tens themselves are *treinta* (30), *cuarenta* (40), *cincuenta* (50), *sesenta* (60), *setenta* (70), *ochenta* (80), *noventa* (90), and *cien* (100).

*Cien* shortens to *cien* exactly at 100, but becomes *ciento* when followed by another number: *ciento uno* (101), *ciento veinte* (120). This one-letter difference is a common spot for learners to slip up.

example.problem: Write out the number 47 and the number 101 in Spanish.
steps: 47 is in the 31+ range, so use the y-pattern: cuarenta (40) + y + siete (7).
101 is over 100, so cien becomes ciento, followed directly by uno with no y.

keyTerms.def: 16; part of the 16-29 range where numbers fuse into single words.
The connecting word used from 31 upward to join tens and units: treinta y uno.
100 on its own is cien; followed by another number it becomes ciento, as in ciento uno (101).
20, the base for the fused 21-29 numbers like veintiuno and veintidós.

practice.q: How do you say 68 in Spanish?
practice.explain: From 31 upward, tens and units are joined with y: sesenta (60) y ocho (8).

practice.q: How do you say 115 in Spanish?
practice.explain: Cien becomes ciento when followed by another number, with no y: ciento quince.

practice.q: Which range of numbers fuses into single words (e.g., dieciséis)?
practice.explain: The teens through twenties (16-29) fuse into single words; from 31 onward, y is used as a separate word instead.

lessons.title: Telling Time and Days of the Week
lessons.intro: Making plans in Spanish means being able to say exactly when — and Spanish tells time with its own small set of rules worth learning once and for all.

sections.heading: Asking and Telling Time
body: To ask the time, say *¿Qué hora es?* Because 'one o'clock' is singular but every other hour is plural, the verb changes: *Es la una* (It's 1:00) uses *es*, but every other hour uses *son*: *Son las dos* (It's 2:00), *Son las tres* (It's 3:00).

For minutes past the hour, add *y*: *Son las tres y media* (3:30, 'and a half'), *Son las cuatro y cuarto* (4:15, 'and a quarter'). For minutes before the next hour, switch to *menos*: *Son las cinco menos cuarto* (4:45, literally 'five minus a quarter').

sections.heading: Days and Months
body: The days of the week are *lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo* — none of them capitalized in Spanish, unlike English. The months are *enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre*, also lowercase.

To say 'on' a day, Spanish uses the definite article instead of a preposition: *el lunes* (on Monday), *los lunes* (on Mondays, every week). Dates are written day-month-year, and 'today is' uses *Hoy es*: *Hoy es el tres de mayo* (Today is May 3rd).

example.problem: How do you say 'It's 4:45' and 'Today is Monday, March 3rd'?
steps: 4:45 is 15 minutes before 5:00, so use menos cuarto with the upcoming hour: Son las cinco menos cuarto.
'Today is' = Hoy es; the date follows day-month order with de linking them: Hoy es lunes, el tres de marzo.
example.answer: Son las cinco menos cuarto. Hoy es lunes, el tres de marzo.

keyTerms.def: The time-telling pattern: es for 1:00, son for every other hour.
'And a half' (:30) and 'and a quarter' (:15), added after the hour.
'Minus a quarter,' used for :45, counted toward the next hour.
'On Monday'; Spanish uses the definite article rather than a preposition to mean 'on' a day.

practice.q: How do you say 'It's 2:00'?
practice.explain: Every hour except 1:00 uses son (plural) plus las: Son las dos.

practice.q: What does 'Son las ocho menos cuarto' mean?
practice.explain: Menos cuarto means 'a quarter before,' so las ocho menos cuarto is a quarter before eight, i.e., 7:45.

practice.q: How do you say 'on Mondays' (every week)?
practice.explain: The plural definite article los lunes expresses a repeated 'on Mondays'; el lunes refers to one specific Monday.

lessons.title: Family and Descriptive Adjectives
lessons.intro: Talking about your family is one of the earliest real conversations you'll have in Spanish, and it's the perfect place to practice adjective agreement with people you actually care about.

sections.heading: Family Vocabulary
body: Core family words: *la madre* (mother), *el padre* (father), *los padres* (parents), *el hermano/la hermana* (brother/sister), *el abuelo/la abuela* (grandfather/grandmother), *el hijo/la hija* (son/daughter), *el tío/la tía* (uncle/aunt), *el primo/la prima* (cousin), *el esposo/la esposa* (husband/wife).

Notice the pattern: the masculine form usually ends in -o and the feminine in -a, matching regular noun gender. *Los abuelos* can mean 'the grandfathers' or, more commonly, 'the grandparents' as a mixed-gender group — Spanish defaults to the masculine plural when a group includes both genders.

sections.heading: Describing People
body: Common descriptive adjectives: *alto/a* (tall), *bajo/a* (short), *delgado/a* (thin), *simpático/a* (nice), *inteligente* (smart, same for both genders), *joven* (young, same for both genders), *viejo/a* (old). Remember: these agree in gender and number with the person described, and usually follow the noun.

*Mi hermana es alta e inteligente* (My sister is tall and smart) shows two adjectives both matching hermana's feminine gender; note that *y* (and) changes to *e* before a word starting with an i-sound, purely for smoother pronunciation.

example.problem: Describe your grandmother as 'short and very nice' in a full Spanish sentence.
steps: Grandmother = mi abuela; use ser for a lasting characteristic.
'Short' = baja (feminine agreement); 'very nice' = muy simpática.
Combine: Mi abuela es baja y muy simpática.
example.answer: Mi abuela es baja y muy simpática.

keyTerms.def: 'The parents' (literally 'the fathers'); Spanish uses the masculine plural for mixed-gender groups.
'Nice' or 'friendly,' a common false-friend-adjacent word (it does not mean 'sympathetic').
The word for 'and' changes from y to e before a word beginning with an i or hi sound, for easier pronunciation.
An adjective like inteligente or joven that doesn't change form for masculine vs. feminine, only for number.

practice.q: What does 'los abuelos' most commonly mean in context?
practice.explain: Spanish defaults to the masculine plural for a mixed-gender group, so los abuelos typically means 'the grandparents.'

practice.q: Which adjective does NOT change form between masculine and feminine?
practice.explain: Inteligente ends in -e and is gender-invariant, only changing for number (inteligentes), unlike alto/alta or bajo/baja.

practice.q: Why does 'y' become 'e' in 'alta e inteligente'?
choices: To avoid two i-sounds colliding before a word starting with i-
Because of the accent mark on alta
practice.explain: Y changes to e before words starting with an i or hi sound purely for smoother pronunciation, similar to a/an in English.

units.title: Present-Tense Verbs and Questions
units.summary: With regular verb patterns and question formation in hand, you can describe daily routines and have real back-and-forth conversations.

lessons.title: Regular -AR Verbs
lessons.intro: Most Spanish verbs end in -ar, and once you learn this one pattern, you can conjugate hundreds of verbs correctly without memorizing each one individually.

sections.heading: The -AR Pattern
body: To conjugate a regular -ar verb, drop the -ar and add: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. Using *hablar* (to speak): *hablo* (I speak), *hablas* (you speak), *habla* (he/she speaks), *hablamos* (we speak), *habláis* (you all speak, Spain), *hablan* (they/you all speak).

This same pattern applies to hundreds of common verbs: *trabajar* (to work) → trabajo, trabajas, trabaja...; *estudiar* (to study) → estudio, estudias, estudia...; *bailar* (to dance) → bailo, bailas, baila... Once the pattern is automatic, new -ar verbs take almost no extra effort.

sections.heading: Using It in Real Sentences
body: The present tense in Spanish covers what English splits into two forms: *hablo español* can mean both 'I speak Spanish' and 'I do speak Spanish' (habitual truth), and with a time word it can even cover the near future: *mañana trabajo* (tomorrow I'm working / I work tomorrow).

Because the verb ending already encodes the subject, sentences routinely drop the pronoun: *Estudiamos mucho* (We study a lot) needs no *nosotros*. The pronoun reappears mainly for emphasis or to avoid ambiguity, such as distinguishing *él habla* from *ella habla*.

example.problem: Conjugate 'bailar' (to dance) for 'we' and 'they,' and use both in a sentence about a party.
steps: Drop -ar from bailar, leaving bail-.
Add -amos for nosotros: bailamos. Add -an for ellos: bailan.
Combine: Nosotros bailamos y ellos bailan en la fiesta.
example.answer: Bailamos y ellos bailan en la fiesta (We dance and they dance at the party).

keyTerms.def: The unconjugated 'to' form of a verb, like hablar (to speak); Spanish infinitives always end in -ar, -er, or -ir.
The set of present-tense endings for regular -ar verbs: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.
The common Spanish practice of omitting the subject pronoun since the verb ending already shows who is acting.
Using the present tense to describe things generally true or regularly done, like hablo español.

practice.q: What is the correct 'nosotros' form of 'estudiar' (to study)?
practice.explain: The nosotros ending for -ar verbs is -amos: estudiar → estudiamos.

practice.q: Why is the subject pronoun often left out of a Spanish sentence?
choices: The verb ending already shows who is acting
Pronouns are only used with -er verbs
practice.explain: Because each verb ending encodes the subject, Spanish speakers typically drop the pronoun unless they need emphasis or clarity.

practice.q: Which form correctly means 'they dance'?
practice.explain: The ellos/ellas/ustedes ending for -ar verbs is -an: bailar → bailan.

lessons.title: Regular -ER/-IR Verbs and Ir, Hacer
lessons.intro: The other two verb families, -er and -ir, share almost identical endings, and two of the most useful irregular verbs, ir and hacer, are worth memorizing on day one.

sections.heading: -ER and -IR Endings
body: Regular -er verbs drop -er and add: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. *Comer* (to eat) → *como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen*. Regular -ir verbs use almost the same endings, differing only in the nosotros/vosotros forms: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en. *Vivir* (to live) → *vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven*.

Notice that -er and -ir verbs share identical endings everywhere except nosotros (-emos vs. -imos) and vosotros (-éis vs. -ís); the yo, tú, él, and ellos forms are identical in shape between the two families.

sections.heading: Ir (to go) and Hacer (to do/make)
body: *Ir* is irregular: *voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van*. It is one of the most useful verbs in the language because *ir a* + infinitive expresses the near future: *voy a comer* (I'm going to eat), exactly like English 'going to.'

*Hacer* (to do/make) is irregular only in the yo form: *hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen*. It is used constantly, including for weather (*hace calor*, it's hot) and asking what someone is doing (*¿Qué haces?*).

example.problem: Say 'I am going to eat pizza' and 'What are you (informal) doing?' in Spanish.
steps: 'Going to' uses ir a + infinitive: voy a + comer.
Add the object: voy a comer pizza.
'What are you doing' uses hacer, tú form: ¿Qué haces?

keyTerms.def: The present-tense endings for regular -er verbs: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en.
The present-tense endings for regular -ir verbs, identical to -er except -imos and -ís.
The 'going to' construction for the near future: voy a comer (I'm going to eat).
'To do/make'; irregular only in the yo form (hago); used for weather and for asking what someone is doing.

practice.q: What is the 'yo' form of 'hacer'?
practice.explain: Hacer is irregular specifically in the yo form: hago, not the expected regular haco.

practice.q: How do you say 'we live' using 'vivir'?
practice.explain: -ir verbs use -imos for nosotros: vivir → vivimos (contrast with -er verbs, which use -emos).

practice.q: Which construction expresses the near future, like 'I'm going to eat'?
practice.explain: Ir a + infinitive (voy a comer) is the standard way to express near-future plans, just like English 'going to.'

lessons.title: Asking Questions and Negation
lessons.intro: Spanish questions are refreshingly simple to form — no auxiliary verbs like English 'do' or 'does' are needed, just intonation, punctuation, and a small set of question words.

sections.heading: Yes/No Questions and Question Words
body: A yes/no question can be formed simply by raising your intonation at the end of a statement, or by inverting subject and verb: *¿Hablas español?* (Do you speak Spanish?) needs no extra 'do.' In writing, Spanish uses an upside-down question mark (¿) at the start and a normal one (?) at the end.

Question words include *qué* (what), *quién* (who), *cuándo* (when), *dónde* (where), *cómo* (how), *por qué* (why), and *cuánto/a* (how much). All question words carry a written accent to distinguish them from similar-looking non-question words, like *que* (that) vs. *qué* (what).

sections.heading: Negation
body: To negate a Spanish sentence, simply place *no* directly before the verb: *No hablo francés* (I don't speak French). Unlike English, there's no separate 'do/does' needed — no does all the negating work by itself.

Double negatives are grammatically correct and required in Spanish, unlike in English: *No tengo nada* (I don't have anything / I have nothing) uses both no and nada together, and dropping either word would sound incomplete or wrong.

example.problem: Ask 'Where do you work?' and answer 'I don't work on Mondays.'
steps: 'Where' = dónde; question form: ¿Dónde trabajas?
Negation: place no directly before the verb: No trabajo...
Add the day with the article: No trabajo los lunes.

keyTerms.def: The upside-down question mark placed at the start of a Spanish question, with a normal one at the end.
The written accent that distinguishes question words like qué, cuándo, dónde from their non-question look-alikes.
The standard way to negate a Spanish sentence: no placed directly before the conjugated verb.
The grammatically required use of two negative words together in Spanish, like no...nada, unlike in standard English.

practice.q: How do you say 'I don't speak French'?
practice.explain: No goes directly before the conjugated verb: No hablo francés, with no extra 'do' needed.

practice.q: Which question word means 'why'?
practice.explain: Por qué means 'why'; qué alone means 'what,' cuándo means 'when,' and cómo means 'how.'

practice.q: Is 'No tengo nada' (I have nothing) correct Spanish grammar?
choices: Yes, double negatives are required in this construction
No, it's a mistake and should be 'Tengo nada'
No, it should be 'No tengo algo'
practice.explain: Spanish requires the double negative no...nada; removing either word would be incomplete or ungrammatical.

units.title: Food, Shopping, and Directions
units.summary: This unit puts your Spanish to work in three of the most common real-world situations: eating out, buying things, and finding your way around.

lessons.title: Food and Ordering: Gustar
lessons.intro: Talking about what you like to eat requires a verb that works backwards from English — master gustar here and you can talk about liking anything.

sections.heading: How Gustar Really Works
body: *Gustar* doesn't mean 'to like' the way English structures it; it literally means 'to be pleasing to.' *Me gusta la pizza* is literally 'Pizza is pleasing to me,' where *la pizza* is the grammatical subject and *me* is the indirect object — the opposite of the English word order.

Because the thing liked is the subject, the verb must agree with it: *me gusta* for one liked thing (*me gusta el café*), but *me gustan* for more than one (*me gustan las manzanas*, I like apples). The indirect object pronoun changes for who's doing the liking: *me, te, le, nos, os, les gusta(n)*.

sections.heading: Food Vocabulary and Ordering Phrases
body: Common food words: *el pan* (bread), *el agua* (water), *la carne* (meat), *el pollo* (chicken), *el arroz* (rice), *las verduras* (vegetables), *la fruta* (fruit), *el café* (coffee). At a restaurant, *quisiera* (I would like, a polite conditional form) is softer than *quiero* (I want): *Quisiera el pollo, por favor*.
Useful ordering phrases: *¿Qué recomienda?* (What do you recommend?) and *La cuenta, por favor* (The check, please). Waitstaff often ask *¿Para tomar?* (To drink?) when taking an order.

example.problem: Say 'I like apples' and 'I would like the chicken, please.'
steps: Apples (manzanas) is plural, so gustar must agree: gustan.
Add the indirect object pronoun me: Me gustan las manzanas.
'I would like' = quisiera + the item + por favor: Quisiera el pollo, por favor.
example.answer: Me gustan las manzanas. Quisiera el pollo, por favor.

keyTerms.def: 'To be pleasing to'; used to express liking, with the liked thing as the grammatical subject.
'I like' (singular/plural thing liked); the verb agrees with the thing being liked, not with 'me.'
'I would like,' a polite way to order or request, softer than quiero (I want).
Pronouns like me, te, le that show who is affected by the verb — required with gustar.

practice.q: Why does 'me gustan las manzanas' use gustan, not gusta?
choices: Manzanas (apples) is plural and is the grammatical subject
Gustan is simply the polite form
It's an irregular exception with no rule
practice.explain: Gustar agrees with the thing liked; since manzanas is plural, the verb takes the plural form gustan.

practice.q: What does 'quisiera' politely mean?
practice.explain: Quisiera is a softened, polite way to say 'I would like,' commonly used when ordering.

practice.q: In 'Me gusta el café,' what is the grammatical subject?
practice.explain: Gustar works backwards from English 'like': the thing pleasing (el café) is the subject, and me is the indirect object.

lessons.title: Shopping, Prices, and Comparisons
lessons.intro: Whether you're haggling at a market or just checking a price tag, a handful of set phrases and one comparison pattern cover almost every shopping situation.

sections.heading: Asking Prices
body: To ask a price, say *¿Cuánto cuesta?* (How much does it cost?, singular item) or *¿Cuánto cuestan?* (for plural items). To describe something as expensive or cheap, use *es caro* (it's expensive) or *es barato* (it's cheap) — with ser, because price and cost are treated as defining characteristics of the item.
Numbers combine directly with currency: *Cuesta veinte dólares* (It costs twenty dollars). *¿Tiene algo más barato?* (Do you have something cheaper?) is a handy phrase for negotiating.

sections.heading: Making Comparisons
body: To compare two things, Spanish uses *más...que* (more...than) and *menos...que* (less...than): *Este es más caro que ese* (This one is more expensive than that one). To say two things are equal, use *tan...como* (as...as): *Es tan bueno como el otro* (It's as good as the other one).

A handful of adjectives have irregular comparative forms instead of using más/menos: *bueno* (good) → *mejor* (better), *malo* (bad) → *peor* (worse), rather than the expected *más bueno* or *más malo*.

example.problem: Say 'This shirt is more expensive than that one, but it's better.'
steps: 'More expensive than' = más caro que: Esta camisa es más caro que esa. (Adjust caro to agree: caro stays if camisa isn't specified as feminine noun agreement — camisa is feminine, so use cara.)
Correct agreement: Esta camisa es más cara que esa.
'But it's better' uses the irregular comparative: pero es mejor.
example.answer: Esta camisa es más cara que esa, pero es mejor.

keyTerms.def: 'How much does it cost?' — the standard way to ask a price in Spanish.
'More...than' / 'less...than,' the standard comparative construction.
'As...as,' used to express equality between two things.
Irregular comparative forms of bueno (good) and malo (bad), used instead of más bueno/más malo.

practice.q: How do you say 'This is more expensive than that'?
choices: Esto es más caro que eso
Esto es caro más que eso
Esto es menos que eso caro
practice.explain: The comparative pattern is más + adjective + que: más caro que.

practice.q: What is the correct comparative for 'good'?
practice.explain: Bueno has an irregular comparative form, mejor (better), rather than the expected más bueno.

practice.q: Which phrase expresses that two things are equal?
practice.explain: Tan...como means 'as...as,' expressing equality, unlike más...que or menos...que which express inequality.

lessons.title: Directions and Prepositions of Place
lessons.intro: Getting lost is inevitable when traveling, but a short list of direction words and place prepositions will get you found again in Spanish.

sections.heading: Giving and Following Directions
body: Key direction words: *a la derecha* (to the right), *a la izquierda* (to the left), *todo derecho* or *todo recto* (straight ahead). The verb *seguir* (to follow/continue) is common in instructions: *Siga todo derecho* (Continue straight ahead, formal command).

*Doblar* means 'to turn': *Doble a la derecha en la esquina* (Turn right at the corner). These formal commands (siga, doble) use the usted form, appropriate for asking a stranger for directions or giving directions politely to one.

sections.heading: Prepositions of Place
body: Useful prepositions: *cerca de* (near), *lejos de* (far from), *entre* (between), *al lado de* (next to), *enfrente de* (in front of/across from), *detrás de* (behind). These all combine with *de* and a noun: *El banco está cerca de la plaza* (The bank is near the plaza).

Because location is always temporary/positional information, all of these phrases pair with *estar*, never ser: *El museo está entre la farmacia y el banco* (The museum is between the pharmacy and the bank).

example.problem: Give directions: 'Go straight, then turn left. The hotel is next to the bank.'
steps: 'Go straight' = Siga todo derecho (formal command).
'Then turn left' = luego doble a la izquierda.
'Next to' uses estar + al lado de: El hotel está al lado del banco.
example.answer: Siga todo derecho, luego doble a la izquierda. El hotel está al lado del banco.

keyTerms.def: 'To the right' / 'to the left,' the core direction phrases.
'To follow/continue' and 'to turn,' the two core direction-giving verbs.
'Next to,' one of several de-based prepositions of place, always paired with estar.
The usted-form instruction (siga, doble) used to politely direct a stranger.

practice.q: Which verb means 'to turn' when giving directions?
practice.explain: Doblar means 'to turn' (doble a la derecha, turn right); seguir means 'to continue/follow.'

practice.q: Why does 'El banco está cerca de la plaza' use estar rather than ser?
choices: Location is expressed with estar, not ser
Cerca is only grammatical with estar
Ser cannot be followed by de
practice.explain: Location is a core estar category (the L in PLACE), so all place prepositions like cerca de pair with estar.

practice.q: What does 'al lado de' mean?
practice.explain: Al lado de means 'next to' or 'beside'; lejos de means 'far from,' and detrás de means 'behind.'

units.title: Past Tense and Real Conversation
units.summary: The final unit adds the preterite tense for talking about completed past events, then pulls everything together into a realistic conversation.

lessons.title: The Preterite: Regular Verbs
lessons.intro: The preterite is the tense you reach for whenever you're telling someone what happened yesterday, last week, or at a specific moment in the past.

sections.heading: Regular -AR Preterite
body: Regular -ar verbs form the preterite by dropping -ar and adding: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. *Hablar* → *hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron*. Notice every ending except nosotros carries a written accent, and that the nosotros form (*hablamos*) is identical in spelling to the present tense — context tells them apart.

The preterite describes a completed, one-time action with a clear beginning and end: *Ayer hablé con mi madre* (Yesterday I spoke with my mother) — the conversation happened and finished, unlike an ongoing or habitual action.

sections.heading: Regular -ER/-IR Preterite
body: Regular -er and -ir verbs share identical preterite endings: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. *Comer* → *comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron*; *vivir* → *viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron*.

Time expressions that signal the preterite include *ayer* (yesterday), *anoche* (last night), *la semana pasada* (last week), and *hace dos días* (two days ago) — all pointing to a finished moment, not an ongoing state.

example.problem: Say 'Yesterday I ate pizza and my sister drank coffee' using the preterite.
steps: 'I ate' from comer, yo form: comí.
'Drank' from beber (a regular -er verb), ella form: bebió.
Combine with ayer: Ayer comí pizza y mi hermana bebió café.
example.answer: Ayer comí pizza y mi hermana bebió café.

keyTerms.def: The Spanish past tense for completed, one-time actions with a clear beginning and end.
-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron, used for regular -ar verbs in the preterite.
-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron, shared by regular -er and -ir verbs in the preterite.
'Yesterday' / 'last night,' common time markers that signal the preterite tense.

practice.q: What is the correct 'yo' preterite form of 'hablar'?
practice.explain: The yo preterite ending for -ar verbs is -é (with an accent): hablé.

practice.q: Which time expression signals the preterite rather than an ongoing action?
practice.explain: Ayer (yesterday) points to a single finished moment, which is exactly what the preterite describes; siempre and todos los días describe habitual, ongoing patterns.

practice.q: What is the 'él/ella' preterite form of 'comer'?
practice.explain: The él/ella preterite ending for -er/-ir verbs is -ió: comer → comió.

lessons.title: Common Irregular Preterites
lessons.intro: A handful of Spanish's most common verbs break the regular preterite pattern entirely — but there are only a few of them, and they're used so often that repetition alone will cement them.

sections.heading: Ir and Ser Share One Form
body: Remarkably, *ir* (to go) and *ser* (to be) share the exact same preterite conjugation: *fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron*. Context alone tells you which verb is meant: *Fui al mercado* (I went to the market, from ir) versus *Fui presidente* (I was president, from ser).
Because these forms carry no accent marks (unlike regular preterites), they're easy to distinguish visually from regular -ar/-er/-ir preterite endings, even before you consider meaning.

sections.heading: Hacer and Tener
body: *Hacer* (to do/make) in the preterite is: *hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron* — note the c→z spelling change in the él/ella form (hizo, not hico) to preserve the correct 's' sound. *Tener* (to have) is: *tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvisteis, tuvieron*.

Both verbs share a pattern common to irregular preterites: no written accents, and a completely different stem from the infinitive (hac- → hic-/hiz-; ten- → tuv-). Once you notice this shared pattern across irregular preterites, new irregular verbs become easier to absorb.

example.problem: Say 'I went to the party and I had a lot of fun' using ir and tener-based vocabulary.
steps: 'I went' from ir, yo form: fui.
'I had a lot of fun' can use tener: tuve mucha diversión, or more naturally, the verb divertirse — for this exercise, use tener: tuve mucha diversión.
Combine: Fui a la fiesta y tuve mucha diversión.
example.answer: Fui a la fiesta y tuve mucha diversión.

keyTerms.def: The shared irregular preterite forms of both ir (to go) and ser (to be); context distinguishes their meaning.
The él/ella preterite form of hacer, with a c→z spelling change to preserve pronunciation.
The yo preterite form of tener, built on the irregular stem tuv-.
A completely different verb stem used in the preterite of certain verbs, unrelated to the infinitive spelling (hacer → hic-).

practice.q: How do you tell apart 'fui' meaning 'I went' from 'fui' meaning 'I was'?
choices: Only from context, since ir and ser share identical preterite forms
By an accent mark that appears only on ser
Ir uses fuí with an accent; ser uses fui without
They are never actually the same word
practice.explain: Ir and ser share the exact same preterite conjugation with no accent marks in either case; only the surrounding sentence reveals which verb is meant.

practice.q: What is the correct él/ella preterite form of 'hacer'?
practice.explain: Hacer's preterite stem is hic-, and the c changes to z before o (hizo) to keep the correct sound; hico would be a spelling error.

practice.q: What is the yo preterite form of 'tener'?
practice.explain: Tener's irregular preterite stem is tuv-, giving tuve for yo, distinct from the present-tense tengo.

lessons.title: Putting It Together: A Real Conversation
lessons.intro: Every piece you've learned — greetings, ser/estar, present tense, gustar, and the preterite — comes together in one realistic exchange you could actually have today.

sections.heading: A Sample Conversation
body: Consider this exchange at a café: *A: ¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás? B: Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? A: Bien también. ¿Qué hiciste ayer? B: Fui al cine con mi hermano. ¿Te gustó la película? A: Sí, me gustó mucho.* Notice estoy (estar, current condition), hiciste and fui (preterite, past events), and me gustó (gustar in the preterite, matching singular película).

This short exchange uses five separate grammar points you've studied across this course, which is exactly how real fluency works: not one grammar rule mastered in isolation, but several woven together naturally in ordinary speech.

sections.heading: Building Your Own Exchange
body: A reliable template for any first conversation: greet (hola/buenos días), ask how someone is (¿cómo estás?), introduce yourself if needed (me llamo...), ask about a recent event using the preterite (¿qué hiciste...?), and react with a gustar-based opinion (me gustó / no me gustó).

From here, expanding your Spanish is mostly a matter of vocabulary, not new grammar structures — the sentence patterns in this course (ser/estar, gustar, present tense, preterite, questions, negation) cover the large majority of everyday conversation you'll encounter.

example.problem: Write a two-line exchange: ask a friend what they did last weekend, and have them answer that they visited their grandmother and it was very nice.
steps: 'What did you do last weekend' = ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana pasado?
'I visited my grandmother' uses the preterite of visitar: Visité a mi abuela.
'It was very nice' uses ser in the preterite: Fue muy agradable.
example.answer: A: ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana pasado? B: Visité a mi abuela. Fue muy agradable.

keyTerms.def: The preterite form of gustar, used to react to a specific past event: 'I liked it.'
'What did you do?' — the preterite question used to ask about a specific past event.
A reusable pattern of greeting, asking a state, asking about a past event, and reacting, useful for any first exchange.
The principle that real fluency comes from weaving multiple grammar points together, not mastering one rule in isolation.

practice.q: In 'Me gustó la película,' what tense is gustó in, and why?
choices: Preterite, because it reacts to one specific, completed viewing
Present, because opinions are always present tense
Future, because gustar always describes the future
It's not a real conjugated form
practice.explain: Gustó is the preterite (él/ella) form of gustar, appropriate because it reacts to one specific, finished event — watching that particular movie.

practice.q: Which question asks specifically about a past action?
practice.explain: ¿Qué hiciste? uses the preterite (hiciste) to ask what someone did at a specific past time; ¿qué haces? asks about the present.

practice.q: According to this lesson, what mostly drives further progress in Spanish after this course?
choices: Vocabulary, since the core grammar patterns are now covered
Learning a completely different grammar system
Abandoning the preterite for a simpler tense
practice.explain: The lesson argues that the grammar patterns taught (ser/estar, gustar, present tense, preterite, questions, negation) cover most everyday conversation, so vocabulary growth becomes the main driver from here.
